identity.title: Training on the Test Task Confounds Evaluation and Emergence

problem.claim: The paper studies how including task-relevant data during pretraining affects evaluation of large language models.

contributions.claim: It defines “training on the test task” as a set of task-relevant pretraining techniques and distinguishes it from malpractice such as test-data training, leakage, or contamination.
It proposes adjusting benchmark comparisons by fine-tuning each compared model on the same task-relevant data before evaluation.
It reports that training on the test task can confound relative model evaluations and claims of emergent capabilities.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a new perspective on language-model evaluation centered on accounting for training on the test task.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that apparent superiority between model families may be explained by different degrees of training on the test task.
The authors report that instances of emergent behavior disappear gradually as models train on the test task.
The authors report that training on the test task confounds both relative model evaluations and emergent-capability claims.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper identifies training on the test task as a fundamental evaluation problem.
It characterizes the practice as task-relevant pretraining data, while distinguishing it from evaluation malpractice.
It argues that unequal exposure to task-relevant training can distort model-family comparisons and emergent-capability claims.
It proposes matched task-relevant fine-tuning before evaluation and reports that instances of emergent behavior disappear gradually as models train on the test task.

source_observation.claim: The paper links a proposed evaluation adjustment directly to the confounding mechanism: equalize task-relevant fine-tuning across compared models before benchmarking.

lessons.interpretation: This offers a concrete claim–evidence alignment pattern: identify a suspected source of comparison bias, then construct a matched-condition adjustment.
lessons.application: When comparing systems exposed to different task-relevant pretraining, add a pre-evaluation matched-data condition and report results before and after adjustment.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when task-relevant data cannot be defined consistently or when matching changes the research question being evaluated.

unknowns: The abstract gives no benchmarks, model details, sample sizes, quantitative effect sizes, or statistical conditions.
The scope and operational definition of “emergent behavior” and the conditions under which it disappears are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish independently verified effectiveness, correctness, reproducibility, or priority of the proposed method.

editorial_revisions.before: It proposes matched task-relevant fine-tuning before evaluation and reports gradual disappearance of emergent behavior under such training.
editorial_revisions.after: It proposes matched task-relevant fine-tuning before evaluation and reports that instances of emergent behavior disappear gradually as models train on the test task.
